the-name.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Yánluó** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "'King Yan' (閻羅, from Yama), the judge of the dead"[^1].

The ASCII form *yanluo* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Yánluó** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves distinctive features the ASCII form loses — the acute accents on á and ó marking the Mandarin tones — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **y** → **Y** — Same letter
- **a** → **á** — Stress mark (acute/tone)
- **n** → **n** — Same letter
- **l** → **l** — Same letter
- **u** → **u** — Same letter
- **o** → **ó** — Stress mark (acute/tone)

The project holds the domain **yánluó.com** (xn--ynlu-5na5i.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Fēngshén Yǎnyì (Investiture of the Gods), various; English abridgment as Creation of the Gods, 1600.
Chinese Buddhist canon (Dàzàngjīng / Taishō Tripiṭaka), Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō (SAT digitization), 1924.

overview.body:
**Yánluó** (*yanluo*) — The Judge Below — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Judgment, Underworld, Order". The name means "'King Yan' (閻羅, from Yama), the judge of the dead"[^1].

Yánluó is the magistrate at the centre of the Chinese afterlife: the Indian god Yama enthroned in a Chinese courtroom, judging the dead from their own record books. Before him, the myth insists, wealth and rank are nothing — the only evidence is what you did.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Yánluó** and serves its temple at [yánluó.com](https://xn--ynlu-5na5i.com). The restoration preserves distinctive features the ASCII form loses — the acute accents on á and ó marking the Mandarin tones — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *yanluo* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
Chinese Buddhist canon (Dàzàngjīng / Taishō Tripiṭaka), Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō (SAT digitization), 1924.
Stephen F. Teiser, The Ghost Festival in Medieval China, Princeton University Press, 1988.

original-script.body:
The original script for this chinese name has not yet been added to PUNICODEX. The form shown is a scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Yánluó** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

Written 阎罗 (simplified) / 閻羅 (traditional): the gate-radical graphs chosen purely for sound, transcribing Yama-. The Chinese name is thus a phonetic fossil of the Silk Road — Sanskrit carried into characters, then naturalized so completely that most speakers never know it was a loanword.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

domains.body:
Yánluó is the magistrate at the centre of the Chinese afterlife: the Indian god Yama enthroned in a Chinese courtroom, judging the dead from their own record books. Before him, the myth insists, wealth and rank are nothing — the only evidence is what you did.[^1]

### The Record Books

The registers of life and death: every deed entered, nothing argued away.

### The Mirror

The karma-mirror that shows each soul its own actions — the courtroom's only witness.

### The Ten Courts

Dìyù's bureaucracy: ten tribunals, his the fifth and most feared.

### The Ledger of Lifespan

He holds the book of allotted years — the deadline no bribe extends.

sources.citation: Chinese Buddhist canon (Dàzàngjīng / Taishō Tripiṭaka), Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō (SAT digitization), 1924.

symbols.body:
The iconography associated with Yánluó concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The judge's cap** — The Chinese magistrate's hat on an Indian god — the Silk Road in one image
- **The brush** — The instrument of the verdict — deaths recorded, sentences written
- **The ox-head and horse-face** — His bailiffs: the two wardens who fetch the souls of the dead

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

mythology.body:
Yánluó's mythology is procedural: not adventures but cases. His stories are judgments — and the judgments are always, the texts insist, simply the soul's own deeds read back to it.[^1]

### Yama, the First Mortal (The Origin)

Before he was a king of hell he was the first man to die: the Ṛgveda's Yama chose mortality, found the road to the other world, and became the guide and host of the fathers — honoured with songs and offerings. Buddhism inherited him as the dharma-king who interrogates the dead: the three messengers — old age, sickness, death — are his summonses, sent to every house.[^2]

### The Fifth Tribunal (The Court)

The Chinese Ten Kings system, formed by the Tang, stations Yánluó in the fifth court — the great reckoning after the first four screenings. There the record books are opened, the mirror of deeds is raised, and the verdict is assigned: paradise, rebirth, or the numbered hells. One legend says he once held the first court but was demoted for leniency — even the king of the dead is audited.

### Bao Zheng on the Bench (The Mercy)

Chinese folklore kept electing incorruptible mortals to his office: the Song-dynasty judge Bao Zheng — "Justice Bao" of a hundred operas — was said to judge the living by day and the dead by night as Yánluó's incarnation. The identification is the myth's message: the perfect magistrate is already doing the underworld's work, and the underworld is only the courtroom made honest.

sources.citation: Chinese Buddhist canon (Dàzàngjīng / Taishō Tripiṭaka), Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō (SAT digitization), 1924.
Stephen F. Teiser, The Ghost Festival in Medieval China, Princeton University Press, 1988.

syncretism.body:
He is the supreme case of Buddhist localization: Yama became Yánluó in China, Enma in Japan (with his own mirror and the red-faced scowl of a thousand temple gates), Yeomna in Korea, and the judges of Vietnamese and Central Asian afterlives. Daoism staffed his courts with its own celestial bureaucrats; folk religion added Mèngpó's tea and the City God as his local deputies. The whole edifice — Indian god, Chinese paperwork, village morality — is East Asia's most successful religious import.[^1]

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[fuxi|Fúxī]], [[guanyin|Guānyīn]], [[long|Lóng]], [[mengpo|Méngpó]], and [[nuwa|Nǚwā]].

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

cultural-legacy.body: "Meeting Yánluó" (见阎罗) remains the everyday Chinese idiom for dying; "Yánwáng ye" names any pitiless authority. Japanese Enma anchors a thousand festivals and anime (Jigoku Shōjo's Enma Ai made him a household name to a new century). The judgment imagery — mirror, ledger, no bribes — shaped East Asian ethics as deeply as any scripture: a whole civilization's conscience, staffed by one borrowed god.[^1]

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

archaeology.body:
The Ten Kings paintings — sets of hanging scrolls showing each court — survive from the Ningbo workshops of the 12th–13th centuries (the finest sets in Nara and the Metropolitan Museum), with Yánluó's tribunal at their dramatic centre. Fengdu ghost city's temples stage the full bureaucratic underworld in statuary. Dunhuang documents preserve the Sūtra of the Ten Kings, the charter-text of the whole system, copied in tens of thousands for the dead's benefit.[^1]

His temples are courtrooms in stone. **Fengdu** ghost city stages his tribunal among the Ten Kings — the judge enthroned above the mirror of deeds, ox-head and horse-face attending — as it has for centuries of Yangtze pilgrims. The **Ten Kings paintings** of the Ningbo workshops (the great sets at Nara and the Metropolitan Museum) fix his iconography: the magistrate's cap, the open register, the mirror raised. In Japan his cult crossed to the great **Enma-dō** halls — Kyoto's Sennyūji among them — where the red-faced king has glared at the faithful for a thousand years.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
Teiser, Ten Kings; the Nara Ten Kings painting corpus.

classical-texts.body:
The judge's titles are all courtroom.

- **Yánluó Wáng (閻羅王)** — 'King Yama'; the full title, Sanskrit worn smooth by Chinese speech.
- **Dìwǔ diàn zhǔ** — 'Lord of the Fifth Court'; his station in the Ten Kings system.
- **Yīn-sī dàshén** — 'Great God of the Dark Office'; the bureaucratic honorific.
- **Yánwáng yé** — 'Grandfather Yama'; the vernacular address, half dread, half familiarity.
- **Enma-ō** — the Japanese form of the title, the same king on the eastern throne.
- **Píngděng wáng** — 'King of Equal Judgment'; one of his doctrinal names: before him, all souls are equal.

sources.citation: Teiser, The Scripture on the Ten Kings; Rigveda 10 (Yama).

daoist-sources.body: The Ten Kings system is Daoism's adopted courtroom: the *Jade Record* (Yùlì) tradition and the Daoist liturgical manuals staff his courts with celestial bureaucrats, assign his registers to the underworld ministries, and integrate his judgments into the funeral liturgy — the priest escorts the soul court by court, with Yánluó's fifth tribunal as the dread center. Daoist vernacular texts make his bureaucracy the afterlife's civil service: seals, registers, petitions, and appeals, the whole machinery of the empire rebuilt underground.

sources.citation: Yùlì bǎochāo; Daoist funerary liturgical manuals.

buddhist-sources.body: His charter is the **Sūtra of the Ten Kings** (*Shíwáng jīng*), the Chinese apocryphon studied by Teiser that built the courts where he judges: the dead pass the ten tribunals at seven-day intervals, and his fifth court, on the thirty-fifth day, is the great reckoning with the mirror and the registers. The Kṣitigarbha (Dìzàng) sūtras share his world — the bodhisattva who vows to empty the hells is his counterweight — and Indian Yama's Ṛgvedic memory, the first mortal who found the road, stands behind every page.

sources.citation: Teiser, The Scripture on the Ten Kings; Ṛgveda 10 (Yama).

calligraphy.body: 阎罗 (閻羅): the graphs are pure phonetics — yán (閻), a gate-radical frame chosen for its sound, and luó (羅), the net-graph already meaning a catch-net — a Sanskrit name (Yama) caught, like the god, in a Chinese net. The transcription is a two-thousand-year-old fossil of the Silk Road, so naturalized that the name feels native; fuller forms 閻羅王 (King Yama) and the clerical variants in the Ten Kings woodblocks show the name's whole journey: a foreign god, spelled into office.

sources.citation: Ten Kings woodblock editions; the transcriptional history of Yama.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/jɛn˧˥ lwo˧˥/** — Mandarin (Hanyu Pinyin with tones).[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: yen-lwoh, rising tone on both syllables.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — 閻羅
- **Full title** — 閻羅王 (Yánluó Wáng)
- **Sanskrit** — Yama
- **Japanese** — Enma
- **Owned form** — Yánluó

Yánluó 阎罗 abbreviates Yánluówáng 阎罗王, "King Yama" — the Sanskrit Yamarāja worn down by two millennia of Chinese speech. The second tone on yán and the rising luó are fixed by tradition; the full Sanskrit form survives in Buddhist ritual language beside the everyday king.

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.

meditation.body:
Yánluó is the god of the life review. His court invents nothing and forgives nothing; it only reads — and the terror and the comfort are the same: the record is exact. He asks the question his mirror has posed for two thousand years: if the book of your deeds were opened tonight, would you need a lawyer — or only a witness?

The records, the mirror, the brush: his court is bureaucracy sanctified, and East Asia read it as a promise as much as a threat — that somewhere, the ledger is accurate and the judge cannot be bought. In a world of imperfect courts, the fifth tribunal stands as the conscience's final appeal: not that punishment will come, but that the truth is on file.

It is fitting that a borrowed god became the conscience of three civilizations: judgment, the myth insists, is not native to anyone — it arrives, it is translated, and it sits down to read the file. The mirror of deeds needs no faith to function; it only needs the one thing every tradition agrees on, that the record should be exact.[^1]

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
